learn: Why one-hot vectors fail and what the analogy test shows
The skip-gram architecture and its softmax objective
Why the full softmax is a bottleneck
Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS): objective, gradients and push–pull dynamics
The noise distribution (counts^0.75) and subsampling of frequent words
GloVe: co-occurrence probability ratios, the weighted least-squares objective and a worked update
intro.why: Word2Vec and GloVe made dense word embeddings practical and showed that meaning can be learned from raw text at scale. Their ideas (self-supervision, negative sampling, the embedding matrix) carry straight into neural language models and Transformers.

symbols: co-occurrence count of words i and j

sections.title: One-hot vectors and the analogy test
sections.plain: Index-based vectors know nothing about similarity; learned embeddings encode relations as directions.
sections.body:
A one-hot vector has a 1 at the word's index and 0 elsewhere. Any two distinct words have dot product 0 (orthogonal), so "hotel" is as unlike "motel" as it is unlike "banana": no notion of similarity, and vectors as long as the vocabulary.

Dense embeddings learned by Word2Vec instead show striking regularities: relations become roughly constant offsets, so

$$\mathbf v_{\text{king}} - \mathbf v_{\text{man}} + \mathbf v_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf v_{\text{queen}}$$

(similarly Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome; walking − walk + swim ≈ swimming). The analogy test became a popular intrinsic evaluation, though regularities are approximate and also reflect corpus biases.

sections.title: Skip-gram: architecture and softmax
sections.plain: Predict each neighbouring word from the centre word with a shallow network.
sections.body:
Slide a window (e.g. ±2) over text; each centre word w and each neighbour c within the window form a training pair. For "the quick brown fox jumps" with window 2 around "fox": (fox, quick), (fox, brown), (fox, jumps), (fox, over).

The network is shallow: a V × D input matrix (rows $\mathbf v_w$, the embeddings we keep) and a D × V output matrix (columns $\mathbf u_c$). Each word therefore has two vectors. The probability of a context word is a softmax over the vocabulary:

$$P(c\mid w) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf u_c^\top\mathbf v_w)}{\sum_{k=1}^{V}\exp(\mathbf u_k^\top\mathbf v_w)},\qquad \mathcal L = -\log P(c\mid w)$$

Training maximises the likelihood of observed context words (cross-entropy loss). Words with similar contexts get similar $\mathbf v$ because they must predict the same $\mathbf u$'s.

sections.title: The softmax bottleneck
sections.plain: Normalising over the whole vocabulary for every pair is far too slow.
sections.body:
The softmax denominator sums over all V words. With V = 100,000 and D = 100, every training pair needs 100,000 dot products (10⁷ multiply-adds) for the forward pass alone, and gradients for every output vector. With billions of pairs this is infeasible.

Security-guard analogy. Instead of asking "which of 100,000 people is this visitor?" (softmax), ask a cheap yes/no question many times: "is this pair (word, context) genuine or a forgery?" That is negative sampling: one real pair and K random fake pairs, i.e. 1 + K dot products (6 with K = 5).

sections.title: Negative sampling: objective and gradients
sections.plain: Make real (word, context) pairs score high and random pairs score low.
sections.body:
SGNS turns prediction into binary classification with the sigmoid, $P(\text{real}\mid w,c) = \sigma(\mathbf u_c\cdot\mathbf v_w)$, and $1-\sigma(x) = \sigma(-x)$. For a positive pair and K negatives $c_1^-\dots c_K^-$ (K = 5–20 for small data, 2–5 for large):

$$\mathcal L = -\log\sigma(\mathbf v_w\cdot\mathbf u^+) - \sum_{k=1}^{K}\log\sigma(-\mathbf v_w\cdot\mathbf u_k^-)$$
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf u^+} = -(1-\sigma(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u^+))\mathbf v,\quad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf u_k^-} = \sigma(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u_k^-)\mathbf v,\quad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf v} = -(1-\sigma^+)\mathbf u^+ + \sum_k\sigma_k^-\mathbf u_k^-$$

Push–pull. The positive context vector is pulled toward $\mathbf v_w$ (and vice versa) in proportion to how wrong the model was; negatives are pushed away. Over many pairs, words with shared contexts converge.

sections.title: Noise distribution and subsampling
sections.plain: Sample negatives from a flattened frequency distribution; randomly skip very common words.
sections.body:
Noise distribution: negatives are drawn from $P_n(w) \propto \text{count}(w)^{3/4}$. The 3/4 power flattens the unigram distribution, so rare words are drawn somewhat more often than their frequency (and "the" somewhat less), which empirically gives better vectors.

Subsampling frequent words: each occurrence of word w in the training text is discarded with probability

$$P_{\text{discard}}(w) = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{t}{f(w)}},\qquad t \approx 10^{-5}$$

where f(w) is the word's frequency. "the" (f ≈ 0.05) is dropped about 99% of the time; rare words never. This speeds training and improves rare-word vectors, since pairs like (fox, the) carry little information.

sections.title: A worked SGNS update
sections.plain: One positive and one negative pair, all numbers by hand.
sections.body:
Centre "king" $\mathbf v = [0.1, 0.3]$; positive context "rules" $\mathbf u^+ = [0.2, 0.9]$; negative "table" $\mathbf u^- = [0.7, 0.1]$; α = 0.1.

  1. Scores: $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u^+ = 0.02 + 0.27 = 0.29$; $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u^- = 0.07 + 0.03 = 0.10$.
  2. Probabilities: σ(0.29) ≈ 0.57, σ(0.10) ≈ 0.52 (the model barely distinguishes them yet).
  3. Errors: positive 1 − 0.57 = 0.43; negative 0.52.
  4. Gradient for v: $-0.43[0.2, 0.9] + 0.52[0.7, 0.1] = [0.278, -0.335]$; $\mathbf v_{\text{new}} = \mathbf v - 0.1\cdot[0.278, -0.335] = [0.0722, 0.3335]$.
  5. $\mathbf u^+_{\text{new}} = \mathbf u^+ + 0.1\cdot0.43\cdot\mathbf v = [0.2043, 0.9129]$; $\mathbf u^-_{\text{new}} = \mathbf u^- - 0.1\cdot0.52\cdot\mathbf v = [0.6948, 0.0844]$.

Code example ex1 reproduces this (exact σ gives [0.0718, 0.3333]), then trains SGNS on a synthetic two-topic corpus: king's nearest neighbours become queen, palace, princess; bread's become spoon, rice, cheese.

sections.title: CBOW and wider windows
sections.plain: Predict the middle word from its averaged neighbours; or sum skip-gram losses over a window.
sections.body:
With window size > 1, skip-gram simply sums the objectives for every (centre, context) pair in the window; the centre vector is pulled toward the centroid of its contexts.

CBOW (continuous bag of words) reverses the direction: average the context vectors $\bar{\mathbf v} = \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{-m\le j\le m, j\ne0}\mathbf v_{t+j}$ and predict the centre word from $\bar{\mathbf v}$ (again with softmax or negative sampling). CBOW is faster and smooths noise; skip-gram does better on rare words and small data because each rare word gets its own predictions.

sections.title: GloVe: co-occurrence ratios
sections.plain: Use the whole corpus's word–word counts; meaning lives in ratios of co-occurrence probabilities.
sections.body:
Count-based methods (LSA/SVD) use global statistics but do poorly on analogies; local-window methods (Word2Vec) capture analogies but ignore global counts. GloVe (global vectors) combines them.

Co-occurrence matrix. "I like cats. I like dogs. I love dogs." with window 1: X(I, like) = 2, X(I, love) = 1, X(like, cats) = 1, X(like, dogs) = 1, X(love, dogs) = 1; so P(like | I) = 2/3. Implementations often weight by 1/d for a pair d words apart.

probe ksolidgaswaterfashion
P(k | ice)1.9×10⁻⁴6.6×10⁻⁵3.0×10⁻³1.7×10⁻⁵
P(k | steam)2.2×10⁻⁵7.8×10⁻⁴2.2×10⁻³1.8×10⁻⁵
ratio8.90.0851.360.96

The ratio is large for words related to ice only (solid), small for steam only (gas), and ≈ 1 for both or neither (water, fashion). GloVe asks for vectors whose differences encode these ratios: $F((\mathbf v_i - \mathbf v_j)^\top\mathbf u_k) = P_{ik}/P_{jk}$; choosing F = exp (a homomorphism turning differences into ratios) gives $\mathbf v_i^\top\mathbf u_k = \log X_{ik} - \log X_i$, with the second term absorbed into biases.

sections.title: GloVe: objective, weighting and comparison
sections.plain: Fit dot products plus biases to log counts, weighting pairs by how much to trust them.
sections.body:
$$J = \sum_{i,j:X_{ij}>0} f(X_{ij})\big(\mathbf v_i^\top\mathbf u_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\big)^2,\qquad f(x) = \begin{cases}(x/x_{\max})^{\alpha} & x < x_{\max}\\ 1 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

with $x_{\max} = 100$, α = 0.75. f gives rare (noisy) pairs little weight, caps very frequent ones, and zero counts are skipped (log 0 undefined), so cost scales with the number of non-zero entries, not V². The final vector for a word is usually $\mathbf v + \mathbf u$.

Worked ("cat"/"milk"): $\mathbf v = [0.5, 0.2]$, $\mathbf u = [0.1, 0.9]$, $b = 0.1$, $\tilde b = 0.3$, f = 0.8, log X = 3, η = 0.05. Prediction 0.05 + 0.18 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.63; error −2.37; J = 0.8 × 2.37² = 4.49. Gradient wrt v: 2·0.8·(−2.37)·u = −3.792u = [−0.3792, −3.4128]; $\mathbf v_{\text{new}} = [0.51896, 0.37064]$; $\mathbf u_{\text{new}} = [0.1948, 0.93792]$; $b_{\text{new}} = 0.2896$. The model raises its prediction toward the observed log count.

Word2Vec (SGNS)GloVe
DataLocal windows, streamedGlobal co-occurrence matrix
ObjectiveBinary classification (real vs noise)Weighted least squares on log counts
CostProportional to corpus sizeProportional to non-zero counts (after one counting pass)
QualityComparable with tuningComparable; strong on analogies

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• SGNS ≈ matrix factorisation: it implicitly factorises a shifted PMI matrix (PMI − log K), linking it to count-based methods.
  • fastText adds character n-grams, so it can build vectors for unseen words from their pieces.
  • Two vectors per word: the input and output vectors differ; most tools keep the input vectors (or their sum with the output vectors).
  • Static embeddings still have one vector per word type; contextual models (M11) fix the polysemy problem.

code.title: Skip-gram with negative sampling from scratch
code.explain: Reproduces the worked update (exact and with rounded σ), then trains 10-dimensional SGNS embeddings on a synthetic two-topic corpus with counts^0.75 negatives and prints nearest neighbours.
mistakes: Updating v with the already-updated u in the same step.
code.notes: Takes ~12 s; real implementations are vectorised and subsample frequent words.
code.code:
"""Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) from scratch, plus the session's worked update.

Synthetic corpus with two 'topics' (royalty and food). Each centre word w has input vector v_w,
each context word c has output vector u_c. For a positive pair and K negatives:
  loss = -log sigma(v.u_pos) - sum_k log sigma(-v.u_neg_k)
"""
import numpy as np
sig = lambda x: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))
# --- worked update (alpha = 0.1, rounded probabilities as in the session)
v, up, un, a = np.array([.1, .3]), np.array([.2, .9]), np.array([.7, .1]), 0.1
sp, sn = v @ up, v @ un
print(f"scores: positive {sp:.2f}, negative {sn:.2f}; sigma: {sig(sp):.3f}, {sig(sn):.3f}")
grad_v = -(1 - sig(sp)) * up + sig(sn) * un
print("dL/dv =", grad_v.round(4), "-> v_new =", (v - a * grad_v).round(4))
print("u_pos_new =", (up + a * (1 - sig(sp)) * v).round(4), " u_neg_new =", (un - a * sig(sn) * v).round(4))
g_r = -(1 - 0.57) * up + 0.52 * un
print("by hand with sigma rounded to 0.57 / 0.52: dL/dv =", g_r.round(3), "-> v_new =", (v - a * g_r).round(4))

# --- train SGNS on a synthetic corpus
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
royal = ["king", "queen", "prince", "princess", "throne", "crown", "palace"]
food = ["bread", "cheese", "soup", "rice", "spoon", "kitchen", "dinner"]
corpus = []
for _ in range(3000):
    topic = royal if rng.random() < 0.5 else food
    corpus += list(rng.choice(topic, 6)) + ["the"]
vocab = sorted(set(corpus)); idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}; V, D, K, win = len(vocab), 10, 5, 2
counts = np.bincount([idx[w] for w in corpus], minlength=V); noise = counts ** 0.75; noise = noise / noise.sum()
Vin, Uout = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (V, D)), np.zeros((V, D)); ids = [idx[w] for w in corpus]; lr = 0.05
for epoch in range(3):
    for i, w in enumerate(ids):
        for j in range(max(0, i - win), min(len(ids), i + win + 1)):
            if j == i: continue
            c = ids[j]; negs = rng.choice(V, K, p=noise)
            v = Vin[w].copy()
            g = (sig(v @ Uout[c]) - 1); Vin[w] -= lr * g * Uout[c]; Uout[c] -= lr * g * v
            for n in negs:
                g = sig(v @ Uout[n]); Vin[w] -= lr * g * Uout[n]; Uout[n] -= lr * g * v
def nn(w, k=3):
    x = Vin[idx[w]]; s = Vin @ x / (np.linalg.norm(Vin, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(x) + 1e-9)
    return [(str(vocab[i]), round(float(s[i]), 2)) for i in np.argsort(-s)[1:k + 1]]
for w in ("king", "bread", "the"): print(f"nearest to {w!r}: {nn(w)}")
print("noise distribution uses counts^0.75: 'the' gets", round(float(noise[idx['the']]), 3), "instead of", round(float(counts[idx['the']] / counts.sum()), 3))

code.title: GloVe: counts, the worked update, and a toy run
code.explain: Builds the window-1 co-occurrence matrix for 'I like cats. I like dogs. I love dogs.', reproduces the worked GloVe update (J = 4.49), then trains GloVe on a two-topic toy count matrix.
code.code:
"""GloVe: co-occurrence counts, the weighted least-squares objective, and the worked update."""
import numpy as np
sents = ["I like cats", "I like dogs", "I love dogs"]
toks = [s.split() for s in sents]; vocab = sorted({w for t in toks for w in t}); ix = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
X = np.zeros((len(vocab),) * 2)
for t in toks:
    for i in range(len(t) - 1):
        X[ix[t[i]], ix[t[i + 1]]] += 1; X[ix[t[i + 1]], ix[t[i]]] += 1      # window 1, symmetric
print("vocab:", vocab); print(X.astype(int))
print("P(like | I) =", X[ix["I"], ix["like"]] / X[ix["I"]].sum())

f = lambda x, xmax=100, al=0.75: (x / xmax) ** al if x < xmax else 1.0
v, u, b, bt, fx, logX, eta = np.array([.5, .2]), np.array([.1, .9]), .1, .3, .8, 3.0, .05
pred = v @ u + b + bt; err = pred - logX; J = fx * err ** 2
print(f"\nworked: prediction {pred:.2f}, error {err:.2f}, J = {J:.2f}")
g = 2 * fx * err
print("grad wrt v =", (g * u).round(4), "-> v_new =", (v - eta * g * u).round(5))
print("u_new =", (u - eta * g * v).round(5), " b_new =", round(b - eta * g, 4))

# train GloVe on a slightly bigger toy corpus
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
royal = ["king", "queen", "prince", "palace", "crown"]; food = ["bread", "soup", "cheese", "kitchen", "spoon"]
words = royal + food; W = len(words); C = np.zeros((W, W))
for _ in range(4000):
    grp = royal if rng.random() < 0.5 else food; a, c = rng.choice(grp, 2, replace=False); C[words.index(a), words.index(c)] += 1
Vm, Um, bv, bu = rng.normal(0, .1, (W, 5)), rng.normal(0, .1, (W, 5)), np.zeros(W), np.zeros(W)
nz = np.argwhere(C > 0)
for it in range(300):
    for i, j in nz:
        e = Vm[i] @ Um[j] + bv[i] + bu[j] - np.log(C[i, j]); gg = 2 * f(C[i, j]) * e
        Vm[i], Um[j] = Vm[i] - .05 * gg * Um[j], Um[j] - .05 * gg * Vm[i]; bv[i] -= .05 * gg; bu[j] -= .05 * gg
E = Vm + Um                                                     # final vectors: sum of both sets
cs = lambda a, b: E[a] @ E[b] / (np.linalg.norm(E[a]) * np.linalg.norm(E[b]))
print(f"\nGloVe toy: cos(king, queen) = {cs(0, 1):.2f}, cos(bread, soup) = {cs(5, 6):.2f}, cos(king, bread) = {cs(0, 5):.2f}")
